items.prose: Sixty IPOs listed last year, and each closed its first day either above its offer price or not. Of the 24 led by a top-tier bank, 18 closed above. Of the other 36, 12 did. A logistic GLM uses one flag, $x = 1$ for a top-tier lead: $\ln\frac{\mu}{1 - \mu} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$.

parts.question: With a single 0/1 flag, the fitted chance in each group equals that group's share. What is $\hat\beta_1$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The top-tier odds are $18/6 = 3$ and the other odds $12/24 = 0.5$, so $\hat\beta_1 = \ln(3/0.5) = \ln 6 \approx 1.7918$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out each group's odds, then compare them on the log scale.

byKey.odds-ratio: That is the odds ratio, 6. The coefficient lives on the log odds scale, so take $\ln 6$.
byKey.share-ratio: You took the log of the ratio of the shares, $0.75/0.3333$. The logit link compares odds, not shares.
byKey.top-only: That is $\ln 3$, the top-tier group's log odds. The slope is its gap from the other group's log odds, $\ln 0.5$.

explain.text: The groups' shares are 0.75 and $\tfrac13$, so their log odds are $\ln 3$ and $\ln 0.5$. The flag's coefficient is the gap between them: $\hat\beta_1 = \ln 6 \approx 1.7918$.

parts.question: Using $\hat\beta_1 = \ln 6$ from part 1, the fitted chances are 0.75 for a top-tier IPO and $\tfrac13$ for the rest. What is the model's residual deviance? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add a log chance for every IPO, those that fell included, then scale the total.

byKey.no-two: That is $-\hat\ell$. The deviance is twice the gap to the saturated model: $D = -2\hat\ell = 72.821$.
byKey.risers-only: You summed only the 30 IPOs that closed above. The 30 that did not add $6\ln 0.25 + 24\ln\tfrac23$ as well.

explain.text: The 18, 6, 12 and 24 IPOs give $\hat\ell = -36.4106$. Each outcome here is a 0 or a 1, so the deviance is $-2\hat\ell \approx 72.821$.

parts.question: With no flag, every IPO gets the pooled chance $30/60 = 0.5$. Using $D = 72.821$ from part 2, what is the likelihood-ratio statistic for the flag? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the deviance of the model with no flag, then take the drop to part 2's model.

byKey.null-only: That is the null deviance, $120\ln 2$. The statistic is its drop to the flag model: $83.178 - 72.821$.
byKey.halved: You took the gap in log-likelihoods. The statistic is twice that gap, the drop in deviance, 10.357.

explain.text: The intercept-only model gives each IPO the chance 0.5, so its deviance is $120\ln 2 = 83.178$. Adding the flag cuts it to 72.821. The drop, 10.357, is the likelihood-ratio statistic.

parts.question: Using the statistic 10.357 from part 3, what is the likelihood-ratio $p$-value? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: One coefficient was added, so compare with $\chi^2_1$: $P(\chi^2_1 > 10.357) \approx 0.0013$. The lead bank's flag matters.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the coefficients the flag adds, then take the upper tail of that $\chi^2$.

byKey.two-df: That uses 2 degrees of freedom. The flag adds one coefficient, so the reference is $\chi^2_1$.
byKey.lower-tail: That is the area below 10.357. The $p$-value is the upper tail, $1 - 0.9987 = 0.0013$.

explain.text: The flag is the only coefficient the larger model adds, so 10.357 is read against $\chi^2_1$. Its upper tail there is about 0.0013. A top-tier lead goes with a first-day rise.

items.prose: An operations team logs failed settlements for ten months. Six domestic months settled 50 thousand trades in all, with 30 fails. Four cross-border months settled 20 thousand trades, with 28 fails. The Poisson GLM is $\ln E[Y_j] = \ln t_j + \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_j$, with $t_j$ the month's trades in thousands and $x_j = 1$ for cross-border.

parts.question: With one 0/1 flag and this offset, each group's fitted fails add up to its observed fails. What is the fitted rate ratio $e^{\hat\beta_1}$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Cross-border fails run at $28/20 = 1.4$ per thousand trades, domestic at $30/50 = 0.6$. The ratio is $1.4/0.6 \approx 2.3333$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn each group's fails into a rate per thousand trades first.

byKey.counts-only: You compared the fail counts, $28/30$, and left out the exposure. Cross-border months settled far fewer trades.
byKey.log-scale: That is $\hat\beta_1 = \ln(7/3)$. The question asks for $e^{\hat\beta_1}$.
byKey.inverted: That is the domestic rate over the cross-border rate. Put cross-border on top.

explain.text: The offset makes the model a model of fails per thousand trades. Each group's fitted rate is its total fails over its total trades, 1.4 and 0.6. So $e^{\hat\beta_1} = 7/3 \approx 2.3333$.

parts.question: Using $\hat\beta_1 = \ln(7/3)$ from part 1, the weights at the fit are $W_j = \hat\mu_j$. They sum to 58 over all months and to 28 over the cross-border months. What is the standard error of $\hat\beta_1$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}$ has rows $(58, 28)$ and $(28, 28)$, determinant 840. The slope entry of the inverse is $58/840$, and $\sqrt{58/840} \approx 0.2628$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Build $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}$ from the two sums, invert it, and read the slope's entry.

byKey.variance: That is the variance, $58/840$. Take its square root for the standard error.
byKey.wrong-entry: You read the intercept's entry, $28/840$. The slope's entry of the inverse is $58/840$.
byKey.no-inverse: You took $1/\sqrt{28}$ from the matrix itself. The standard error needs the inverse, whose slope entry is $58/840$.

explain.text: With columns $(1, x)$ and $W = \hat\mu$, $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 58 & 28 \\ 28 & 28 \end{pmatrix}$. Its inverse has slope entry $58/(58 \times 28 - 28^2) = 58/840$. The standard error is $\sqrt{58/840} \approx 0.2628$.

parts.question: The model's Pearson statistic is 17.6, from ten months and two coefficients. Using the standard error 0.2628 from part 2, what is the quasi-Poisson $z$ for $\hat\beta_1 = 0.8473$? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\hat\phi = 17.6/8 = 2.2$, so the standard error grows to $\sqrt{2.2 \times 58/840} = 0.38975$ and $z = 0.84730/0.38975 \approx 2.174$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Estimate the dispersion from the Pearson statistic, then scale the standard error by it.

byKey.poisson-z: That is the plain Poisson $z$, $0.8473/0.2628$. The fails spread more than a Poisson allows, so scale the standard error first.
byKey.phi-not-root: You multiplied the standard error by $\hat\phi = 2.2$. The variance scales by $\hat\phi$, so the standard error scales by $\sqrt{2.2}$.
byKey.ten-df: You divided 17.6 by 10. Two coefficients were fitted, so the residual degrees of freedom are $10 - 2 = 8$.

explain.text: Ten months less two coefficients leave 8 degrees of freedom, so $\hat\phi = 17.6/8 = 2.2$. The estimate 0.8473 stands, but its standard error grows by a factor of $\sqrt{2.2}$, to 0.38975. So $z = 0.84730/0.38975 \approx 2.174$.

parts.question: Take the quasi-Poisson standard error 0.38975 from part 3. What is the lower end of a 95% interval for the rate ratio? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: On the log scale the interval starts at $0.84730 - 1.96 \times 0.38975 = 0.0834$, and $e^{0.0834} \approx 1.087$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Build the interval for $\beta_1$ first, then map its end back to a ratio.

byKey.poisson-se: That uses the Poisson standard error 0.2628. With the dispersion of 2.2 the interval is wider, from $e^{0.0834}$.
byKey.log-scale: That is the end on the log scale, 0.0834. Exponentiate it to read a rate ratio.

explain.text: The interval for $\beta_1$ is $0.84730 \pm 1.96 \times 0.38975$, so it starts at 0.0834. Exponentiating gives a rate ratio of at least about 1.087. Cross-border fails run above the domestic rate even after the extra spread.

items.prose: A back office counts its reconciliation breaks on six days: 0, 6, 2, 5, 1 and 4. It fits a Poisson GLM with a log link and an intercept only, $\ln\mu = \beta$, by IRLS from $\beta = 0$.

parts.question: All six fitted means are equal, so each update sets $\beta$ to the plain average of the working responses. What is $\beta$ after the first update? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: At $\beta = 0$, $\mu = 1$, so each $z = 0 + (y - 1)/1$. Their average is $3 - 1 = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write the working response for a Poisson count with a log link at $\mu = 1$, then average it.

byKey.mean-count: That is the average count, $\bar y = 3$. The update averages $z = \eta + (y - \mu)/\mu$, which at $\mu = 1$ is $y - 1$.
byKey.jump-to-fit: That is $\ln 3$, where the loop ends. One step from 0 lands at the average of $y - 1$, which is 2.

explain.text: At $\beta = 0$ every day has $\mu = 1$, so its working response $\eta + (y - \mu)/\mu$ is just $y - 1$. The six days share one weight, so the update is the average of $y - 1$: $3 - 1 = 2$.

parts.question: Using $\beta^{(1)} = 2$ from part 1, what is $\beta^{(2)}$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Recompute $\mu$ at $\beta = 2$, then average the working responses again.

byKey.no-eta: You averaged $(y - \mu)/\mu$ alone. The working response starts from the current $\eta = 2$.
byKey.sign: You added the correction with the wrong sign. The fit at $\beta = 2$ overshoots the data, so $\beta$ falls.

explain.text: Averaging $z = \beta + (y - \mu)/\mu$ gives $\beta_{\text{new}} = \beta + (\bar y - \mu)/\mu$. At $\beta = 2$ that is $2 + (3 - e^2)/e^2 = 1.4060$.

parts.question: Using $\beta^{(2)} = 1.4060$ from part 2, the updates keep falling and settle. What value does $\beta$ converge to? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The loop stops where $(\bar y - \mu)/\mu = 0$, that is $\mu = 3$. So $\hat\beta = \ln 3 \approx 1.0986$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask where the update stops changing $\beta$.

byKey.mean-scale: That is the fitted mean $\hat\mu = 3$. The log link puts $\hat\beta = \ln 3$ on the linear scale.
byKey.one-more: That is $\beta^{(3)}$, one step on from 1.4060. Two more steps settle at $\ln 3 = 1.0986$.

explain.text: The update is $\beta + (\bar y - e^\beta)/e^\beta$, which stops changing when $e^\beta = \bar y = 3$. So the loop settles at $\ln 3 \approx 1.0986$, the Poisson maximum likelihood fit.

parts.question: Using $\hat\mu = e^{1.0986} = 3$ from part 3 for every day, what is the Pearson dispersion estimate, $\chi^2$ over its residual degrees of freedom? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Sum $(y - \hat\mu)^2/\hat\mu$, then divide by the days less the one coefficient.

byKey.six-df: You divided by 6. One coefficient was fitted, so there are 5 residual degrees of freedom.
byKey.chi-only: That is the Pearson statistic itself. Divide it by its 5 degrees of freedom.

explain.text: Each day adds $(y - 3)^2/3$, and the six terms total 9.3333. One coefficient leaves 5 degrees of freedom, so $\hat\phi = 1.8667$. The breaks spread almost twice as much as a Poisson count would.

items.prose: A gilt desk records whether each auction tails, clearing below the price the market expected. A logistic GLM on the bid-to-cover ratio $c$ gives $\hat\mu = 1/(1 + e^{-(2.6 - 1.3c)})$.

parts.question: At what bid-to-cover ratio is a tail as likely as not? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: A chance of one half needs $\eta = 0$, so $2.6 - 1.3c = 0$ and $c = 2.6/1.3 = 2.0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which value of $\eta$ gives a chance of one half.

byKey.intercept: That is the intercept, 2.6. The chance is one half where the whole $\eta = 2.6 - 1.3c$ is 0.

explain.text: The inverse logit gives one half exactly when its argument is 0. Here $\eta = 2.6 - 1.3c$, which is 0 at $c = 2.0$. A thinner cover than that makes a tail the likelier outcome.

parts.question: Using the even-odds cover $c = 2.0$ from part 1, a cover of 2.5 sits 0.5 above it. What is the chance of a tail at 2.5? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find $\eta$ at $c = 2.5$, then put it through the inverse logit.

byKey.sign: You used $1/(1 + e^{-0.65})$, which flips the sign of $\eta$. The minus in the exponent meets $\eta = -0.65$.
byKey.linear: That is the linear predictor $\eta$. Put it through the inverse logit to get a chance.

explain.text: The linear predictor is $\eta = 2.6 - 3.25 = -0.65$. The inverse logit maps it to $1/(1 + e^{0.65}) \approx 0.3430$.

parts.question: Using $\hat\mu = 0.3430$ from part 2, what variance does the Bernoulli family give one auction's outcome? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the Bernoulli variance function.

byKey.poisson-var: That is the Poisson variance function, $V(\mu) = \mu$. A 0/1 outcome has $\mu(1 - \mu)$.
byKey.gamma-var: That is $\mu^2$, the Gamma variance function. A 0/1 outcome has $\mu(1 - \mu)$.

explain.text: An auction either tails or it does not, with chance 0.3430 of a tail. A 0/1 outcome with that chance has variance $0.3430 \times 0.6570 \approx 0.2253$.

parts.question: Next quarter brings 12 auctions, each expected near a cover of 2.5, with independent outcomes. Using the variance 0.2253 from part 3, what is the standard deviation of the number of tails? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the 12 variances, then take a square root.

byKey.variance: That is the variance of the count, $12 \times 0.2253$. Take its square root.
byKey.one-auction: That is one auction's standard deviation. The count adds 12 independent outcomes, so add 12 variances.
byKey.poisson: You gave each auction the variance 0.3430, as a Poisson would. A 0/1 outcome has $\mu(1 - \mu) = 0.2253$.

explain.text: The count of tails is a sum of 12 independent 0/1 outcomes, each with variance 0.2253. The variances add to 2.7042. Its square root, 1.644, is the standard deviation, against a mean of 4.12.
